overview: Both magnify specimens, but they use different sources (light versus electrons) giving very different resolution and sample requirements.
genZNote: Light microscopy: see the neighbourhood. Electron microscopy: zoom in to see individual bricks.

aspects.label: Illumination Source
aspects.valueA: Visible light, focused through glass lenses.
aspects.valueB: A beam of electrons, focused using electromagnetic lenses.

aspects.label: Resolving Power
aspects.valueA: Limited resolution, around 200 nm; can't distinguish structures smaller than that.
aspects.valueB: Much higher resolution, down to about 0.1-0.2 nm — can visualise viruses and organelle detail.

aspects.label: Sample Requirements
aspects.valueA: Can view living or stained samples with minimal preparation.
aspects.valueB: Requires extensive preparation (fixation, dehydration, coating) and is usually performed on dead, non-living samples in a vacuum.

aspects.label: Cost / Accessibility
aspects.valueA: Relatively inexpensive and widely available, including in student labs.
aspects.valueB: Expensive, specialised equipment, generally limited to research settings.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Viruses are too small to be seen with a light microscope — visualising them requires an electron microscope.
overlay.memoryTrick: Light micro = see cells and bacteria. Electron micro = see viruses and fine organelle detail.
overlay.commonMisconception: Electron microscopy cannot be used on living samples — the vacuum and preparation process kills the specimen, unlike light microscopy.
